title: Instructional Coaching - the New New Thing
author: Dominic Salles
summary: Dominic Salles argues, in his deliberately nuance-free style, that schools should not launch instructional coaching because it will not scale and the time and money would buy more elsewhere. Responding to Robert Coe's reservations, he proposes getting the benefit without the programme: choose six to eight techniques, such as Tracking Not Watching, and teach them to whole departments through short rhetorical questions and CPD. He then replaces observation and coaching conversations with a simple 30-day teacher journal of dots, ticks and hearts. The piece closes with a rule for imperfect rollout: find the main barrier, make one change, go again. It is a provocative practitioner case for scalable PD, written in opposition to research-style caveats.
points: Salles contrasts the professor's habit of weighing evidence with the practitioner's need to commit, claiming nuance in schools preserves the status quo.
Coaching is slow and costly because it depends on visits, feedback crafting and one-to-one conversations.
A short list of six to eight techniques taught to whole departments scales where one-to-one coaching does not.
A thirty-day self-monitoring journal lets a teacher build a habit without further lesson visits.
Imperfect implementation is handled by reviewing early, removing the main barrier, and repeating until good enough.
quotes: Nuance in the classroom just means the status quo, as there we can justify any position. The jury is always out. So the status is always quo.

If you are thinking of doing instructional coaching in school, don’t do it. It won’t work at scale. And even if it does, other things you could have done with the immense use of time and money would get you better results, more quickly.

Imagine your school has looked at the 62+ Teach Like a Champion techniques, and picked 6-8 which will become staples of CPD and classroom practice. Or you have picked them from Rosenshine. Or wherever, you’ve got some.
But, that’s a lot to keep in the teacher’s head. It also relies on someone visiting the lesson, watching it, crafting the feedback, and having the coaching conversation. Slow and expensive.

I don’t have to keep visiting the lessons. I can easily ask the teacher at any time what they notice about their journal. Or we can do it in a department meeting. Or teachers can have that conversation with each other.
This is scaleable for every department and for every teaching technique. That’s why you only have 6-8. Nuance is for wimps.
